Seminar Title:

A Resolution-Dependent Decomposition of Machine Learning Skill in Urban Streamflow Prediction

Seminar Type:

Departmental Seminar

Department:

Civil Engineering

Speaker Name:

Prachi Pragyan Mahanta

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Seminar Hall, Department of Civil Engineering

Date and Time:

03 Sep 2026 05:00 PM

Contact:

Dr. Ratnakar Swain

Abstract:

Machine learning (ML) models for urban streamflow prediction frequently report Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) exceeding 0.95, yet these metrics are rarely decomposed across temporal resolutions to assess whether skill originates from hydrological learning or statistical artifacts. This study presents the first dual resolution performance decomposition, systematically disentangling temporal autocorrelation, station memorization, and meteorological signal at daily (5,470 records) and hourly (130,349 records) timescales using five USGS urban stations in the Baltimore metropolitan area (2022-2024). Random Forest regressors were evaluated under six experimental configurations with random-seed sensitivity analysis (n=10). The results reveal a resolution paradox: hourly persistence achieves NSE = 0.984 with flow lags constituting 98.8% of permutation importance, while the full RF model (NSE = 0.965) underperforms persistence. At daily resolution, persistence drops to NSE = 0.775 and static catchment features dominate importance (71.6%), with meteorological features contributing 21.1%. This features importance inversion where finer resolution strengthens persistence dominance rather than revealing meteorological signal challenges the assumption that sub-daily data enables ML to capture rainfall-runoff dynamics. Met-only RF achieves similar NSE at both scales (0.25), indicating resolution-invariant meteorological signal. Leave-One-Station Out cross-validation confirmed spatial generalization limitations (daily avg NSE = -0.40; hourly avg NSE = -1.63). These findings establish that ML evaluation conclusions are fundamentally resolution-dependent and recommend three evaluation standards: resolution-specific persistence baselines, feature group ablation, and spatial cross-validation.
